senses.def: the Hebrew name for the ruling angel in Hell; see 93.32
Herod Agrippa II, the son of Herod Agrippa I (see Acts 12:1)
the process of causing blood to flow out
senses.comment: It may be important in translating Hebrews 9:22 to introduce some statement with regard to sacrifice, for example, ‘if the blood of the sacrifice did not flow’ or ‘if there was no sacrifice involving blood’ or simply ‘if there was no sacrifice,’ but because of the symbolic value of ‘blood’ in the ritual, some reference to blood should be retained.

senses.def: pertaining to strict conformity to a norm or standard, involving both detail and completeness
pertaining to one who has not acquired a formal education, and hence with the implication of being stupid and ignorant
to bring or lead up
to bring an offering to
to begin to go by boat
senses.comment: In some languages a distinction is made in putting out to sea based upon whether the boat goes out from a beach and thus passes through waves or whether it goes out to sea from a harbor. In the various contexts of the book of Acts it is preferable to use a term which implies a harbor, while in contexts which speak of the Sea of Galilee, movement would normally be from a beach (see 54.5).

senses.def: to pull or draw something in an upward direction
senses.comment: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made on the basis of the means by which something is pulled or drawn. For example, to pull something by means of a rope may be entirely different from a term indicating that the object itself has been seized and is being drawn or dragged.

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause someone to stand up
to cause someone to live again after having once died
(an idiom, literally: to raise up seed) the male role in begetting children
senses.comment: In contexts such as Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:19, and Luke 20:28 it may be important to add a note concerning levirate responsibilities, that is to say, the requirement for a younger brother to beget children by a deceased older brother’s wife and the reckoning of such an offspring as being the descendant of the older deceased brother.

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to assume a standing position
to move away from a reference point, with the possible implication of ‘getting up and leaving’
to come into existence, with the implication of assuming a place or position
to come back to life after having once died
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’

senses.def: to rise up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands
pertaining to having a relatively high degree of comparable merit or worth
pertaining to being fitting or proper in corresponding to what should be expected
to register someone, often in connection with taking a census
glosses: to put on a census list
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ἀπογράφω is simply ‘to have one’s name put in a book’ or ‘to have one’s name put in a list of those living in a particular place.’|In Hebrews 12:23 (καὶ ἐκκλησίᾳ πρωτοτόκων ἀπογεγραμμένων ἐν οὐρανοῖς ‘and at the gathering of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven’) ἀπογράφω is used in a figurative sense, but it is usually translated more or less literally.

senses.def: to cause someone to depart for a particular purpose
to send a message, presumably by someone
(an idiom, literally: to send a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of ἄριστον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of ἄριστον[b], 23.23)
senses.comment: Though ἄριστον[a], δεῖπνον[a], and βρῶσις[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of Mark 6:21 that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

senses.def: a less important meal, normally in the earlier or middle part of the day
a high-ranking official in Asia Minor (in an area which is now Turkey)

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day following the day of a discourse

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time subsequent to another point of time and indicating imminence, that is to say, the subsequent event is regarded as almost begun
to cause to be deep
to move slowly by boat
(derivative of γίνομαι[c] ‘to become,’ 13.48) that which is a product or result of becoming
(derivative of δαιμόνιον[a] ‘demon,’ 12.37) pertaining to a demon
senses.comment: In some languages δαιμονιώδης may be rendered as ‘typical of the way a demon acts’ or ‘the way in which demons behave.’

senses.def: extension toward a goal at or near the speaker and implying movement

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time simultaneous with another point of time, but with the possible implication of a particular set of circumstances
to cause the spread or extension of something
(a figurative extension of meaning of διανέμομαι ‘to spread out,’ not occurring in the NT) to become known as the result of information spreading abroad
to acquire information by questioning
glosses: to find out about by inquiry
senses.comment: Since πυνθάνομαι[b] and διερωτάω imply quite distinct semantic components, namely ‘to acquire information’ and ‘by the process of questioning,’ it may be appropriate in many languages to use two verbs meaning ‘to ask’ and ‘to find out.’ Accordingly, this expression in Acts 10:17 may be rendered as ‘meanwhile, men sent by Cornelius asked and learned where Simon’s house was.’

senses.def: the quality of splendid, remarkable appearance
the state of brightness or shining
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between some object which is bright in and of itself (that is to say, the source of brightness or radiance) and objects which are bright because they reflect light from some source. In the case of Matthew 17:5 (which is generally regarded as a reference to the Shekinah presence of God), the cloud would not be merely reflecting light but would be a source of light (see 14.50).|In Revelation 15:8 (καὶ ἐγεμίσθη ὁ ναὸς καπνοῦ ἐκ τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ ‘and the temple was filled with smoke from the brightness of God’) the reference is evidently to the Shekinah. The Shekinah, which filled the Temple when it was first constructed (), was regarded as a bright, cloud-like object which represented the personal presence of God.

senses.def: a manifestation of power characterized by glory
senses.comment: In some languages the aspect of ‘glorious’ may be expressed as ‘that which causes wonder’ or ‘that which causes people to marvel.’

senses.def: to speak of something as being unusually fine and deserving honor

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: honor as an element in the assignment of status to a person

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a state of being great and wonderful
a benevolent supernatural power deserving respect and honor
senses.comment: If one can employ a phrase such as ‘wonderful beings above,’ this is fine, but in a number of languages such a phrase would refer to believers who have died. Since the reference is apparently to certain types of supernatural powers, it may be more satisfactory in some languages to speak of ‘the glorious spirits above.’

senses.def: a place which is glorious and as such, a reference to heaven
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, interpret δόξα in 1 Timothy 3:16 as an abstract and thus translate ἐν δόξῃ as ‘in a glorious way’ or ‘in a wonderful way’ or ‘in a way that revealed his glory.’

senses.def: the reason or basis for legitimate pride

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause to stand up, with a possible implication of some previous incapacity

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to get up, normally from a lying or reclining position but possibly from a seated position (in some contexts with the implication of some degree of previous incapacity)
to cause someone to awaken
to cause to come into existence
to cause someone to live again after having once died
senses.comment: In some languages it may be important to indicate in Matthew 28:6 who is the agent, and one may therefore translate ‘he is not here; God has caused him to live again.’

senses.def: to change to a previous good state
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐγείρω[a] ‘to cause to stand up,’ 17.10) to restore a person to health and vigor (somewhat equivalent to the English idiom to get him on his feet again)
to become awake after sleeping
senses.comment: The context of this clause in Romans 13:11 is figurative, and it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘now it is time for you to be alert to what is happening.’

senses.def: to go to war against
glosses: to rise up in arms against

senses.def: to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
senses.comment: εἰσέρχομαι[a] is also used in the NT in speaking of the entrance of demons or Satan into animate beings, for example, λέγοντες, Πέμψον ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς χοίρους, ἵνα εἰς αὐτοὺς εἰσέλθωμεν saying, Send us into the swine so we may enter them Mark 5:12. In a number of languages one cannot speak of such supernatural beings ‘entering’ an object. It may be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to grab’ or ‘to control’ or ‘to command.’

senses.def: to happen, with the focus upon the initial aspect
senses.comment: In some languages it may be impossible to speak of ‘sin coming’ (Romans 5:12), and therefore one may have to restructure the relationships, for example, ‘people began to sin.’

senses.def: to begin, with the focus upon the initial stages of an activity
senses.comment: In the first clause of Luke 9:46, it is clear that the event is to be found in the noun διαλογισμός, while the verb εἰσῆλθεν merely contributes an aspect of the event.

senses.def: to begin to experience an event or state
(idiom, literally: to go in and to go out) to live or to conduct oneself in relationship to some community or group
senses.comment: The semantic focus of this idiom in Acts 1:21 appears to be the manner in which a person conducts himself in relationship to others, but it is possible to imply a certain amount of movement. For example, in Acts 1:21, it is possible to translate ‘during the whole time the Lord Jesus travelled about with us.’

senses.def: to cause something to become dry by wiping with a dry substance
to cause to become visible
to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐμφανίζω in Acts 23:22, see 33.208.

senses.def: to reveal something which is not generally known
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐμφανίζω in Acts 23:22, see 28.36.

senses.def: to make a formal report before authorities on a judicial matter
preparation of a body for burial
one who drives out evil spirits, usually by invoking supernatural persons or powers or by the use of magic formulas
(derivative of ἐπερωτάω[b] ‘to ask for,’ 33.161) that which is asked for
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐπερώτημα in 1 Peter 3:21 as meaning ‘pledge’ or ‘promise,’ in which case it may be classified under 33.288. Accordingly, the phrase συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς θεόν may be rendered as ‘a promise made to God from a good conscience.’

senses.def: to long for something, with the implication of recognizing a lack
to experience a yearning affection for someone
glosses: to have a great affection for
to have a yearning love for
senses.comment: The nominal phrase with the English term ‘affection’ can and must be expressed in a number of languages by verb phrases or clauses. In 2 Corinthians 9:14 one may translate ‘they love you very much and will pray for you.’

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are seven instances of a countable entity
senses.comment: In ancient times, seven was regarded as a particularly important sacred number, and this is especially relevant in a number of passages in the book of Revelation.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to having high status, with the possible implication of special family relations contributing to such status
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 1:26, it is somewhat unlikely, though not impossible, that hereditary status is involved.

senses.def: a willingness to learn and evaluate something fairly
a river in Mesopotamia
ruling over, with the implication of providing direction and leadership
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to express the concept of ‘ruling’ by some form of ‘command,’ for example, ‘he commands people what they must do’ or ‘he orders people’ or ‘he is the chief over people.’

senses.def: to cause someone to be publicly exhibited as an object of shame or disgrace
immediate female offspring
senses.comment: A literal rendering of Matthew 10:37, namely, ‘whoever loves his son or daughter more than me,’ may be misleading, since in some languages it could refer to only one particular son or daughter. A more indefinite expression may therefore be preferable, namely, ‘any one of his sons or daughters.’

senses.subdomain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θυγάτηρ[a] ‘daughter,’ 10.46) a woman for whom there is some affectionate concern
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate θυγάτηρ[b] literally as ‘daughter,’ since this would imply that Jesus was acknowledging that the woman was in fact his own daughter. An obvious adjustment must be made in such instances, and therefore one may use such expressions as lady or my dear woman.

senses.def: (an extended meaning of θυγάτηρ[a] ‘daughter,’ 10.46) a nonimmediate female descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations)
senses.comment: See discussion at υἱός[c] 10.30 and its footnote.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θυγάτηρ[a] ‘daughter,’ 10.46) a female inhabitant of a place

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: daughter of Zion) the inhabitants of Jerusalem
a state of happiness characterized by being cheerful
senses.comment: In some languages ‘cheerfulness’ may be expressed idiomatically as ‘one’s heart is laughing’ or ‘one’s eyes are dancing.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: one who customarily engages in doing what is bad
to invoke divine harm if what is said is not true or if one does not carry out what has been promised
senses.comment: See discussion of Mark 14:71 (ἀναθεματίζω 33.472).

senses.def: a construction built by birds in connection with brooding and raising their young
senses.comment: It is possible to understand κατασκήνωσις in Matthew 8:20 as simply a sheltered place, but the most natural interpretation would appear to be ‘nest.’

senses.def: to express an unusually high degree of confidence in someone or something being exceptionally noteworthy
senses.comment: Whether in any particular context the boasting is legitimate or not depends upon what is boasted about. In a number of languages, however, quite different terms are employed, depending upon the differing degrees of justification for such boasting.

senses.def: to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
to cease, in reference to some type of movement
senses.comment: Languages may differ considerably in expressions relating to the ceasing of wind, for example, ‘the wind died,’ ‘the wind stood still,’ ‘the wind refused to move,’ or ‘the wind could not be felt.’

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved
(derivative of Λαοδίκεια ‘Laodicea,’ 93.514) a person who lives in or is a native of Laodicea
arguing or quarreling about the meaning or use of words
(derivative of μακροθυμία ‘patience,’ 25.167) to demonstrate patience despite difficulties

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend a period of time on the basis of a particular mental attitude

senses.comment: Expressions for a number of terms for color differ on the basis of the object which is designated as having such a color. For example, a term for black as applied to a horse may be a different term from what one would use in speaking of a black box.

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: a dark liquid used in writing or marking
senses.comment: The use of ink is so universal at the present time that some term or expression for it is almost inevitable in all languages. However, in some cases the equivalent is essentially a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘black stain’ or ‘writing stain.’

senses.def: act of causing someone to change a place of habitation
a degree which almost equals some point on a scale of extent, but not quite
one who owns a ship
senses.comment: For an illustrative example, see Acts 27:11 in 54.28.

senses.def: the young of any bird
any type of building or structure which encloses an area, but the area may be open to the sky, as in the case of amphitheaters
the construction of something, with focus on the event of building up or on the result of such an event
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 3:9 the phrase θεοῦ οἰκοδομή has been interpreted by many as ‘a dwelling place for God’ (see 7.1), but it is more likely that the Christian is regarded as the result of God’s activity, that is to say, the believer is ‘God’s construction’ or ‘that which God has made.’ οἰκοδομή in 2 Corinthians 5:1 (οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ θεοῦ ἔχομεν ‘we have a construction from God’) may be regarded as having essentially the same meaning as in 1 Corinthians 3:9, though the reference here is to the glorified body.

senses.def: to increase the potential of someone or something, with focus upon the process involved
act of speaking disparagingly of a person in a manner which is not justified
the scent or odor of a substance, whether agreeable or disagreeable
to provide instruction, with the intent of forming proper habits of behavior
to train someone in accordance with proper rules of conduct and behavior
to punish for the purpose of improved behavior

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to bend over or stoop down, with the implication of looking into something
to look into something by stooping down
(a figurative extension of meaning of παρακύπτω[b] ‘to stoop and look into,’ 24.13) to make considerable effort in order to try to find out something

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (derivative of παροικέω[b] ‘to live as a foreigner,’ 85.78) a person who for a period of time lives in a place which is not his normal residence
senses.comment: In Acts 7:6 the expression ‘as strangers in a foreign country’ may be rendered ‘as strangers living in a country which was not their own.’ Similarly, ‘who live as aliens’ may also be rendered as ‘who live in countries not their own’ or ‘who live with people to whose nation they do not belong.’

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are fifty instances of a countable entity
rubbish, resulting from the process of cleansing

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: the overflowing of the banks by a river or stream
senses.comment: One might very well render Luke 6:48 as ‘when the river overflowed its banks, it burst against the house.’ In some instances it may not be possible to use a term which would be more or less literally ‘to burst against,’ but one can say ‘tried to cause the house to collapse’ or ‘tried to destroy the house.’

senses.def: the person who had the principal authority on the island of Malta
herbivorous domestic mammal with four legs; Ovis ladicaudata - fat-tailed sheep; used for sacrifice, source of meat, milk, hides, wool, and horns
senses.comment: Since the distribution of sheep throughout the world is somewhat less than that of goats, there may be more difficulties involved in finding an adequate term. In some instances terms for sheep are actually based upon a term for goat. For example, among Eskimos goats are well known because there are wild goats in the mountains, and sheep are accordingly called in some dialects ‘woolly goats’ or ‘goats that have wool.’ Among the Maya in Yucatan sheep were introduced by the Spanish and were first described as being ‘cotton deer,’ and the name still persists. In some areas where sheep are not known at all, the meat of sheep is known, and accordingly sheep may be called by the name of the meat, for example, ‘mutton animals.’ But in most places where sheep are not indigenous, there is nevertheless some term for them, usually based upon a borrowing from a dominant language.|For the translator, however, there are often problems involving the connotations of the term for sheep and for related expressions concerning their behavior and the ways in which they are ‘led.’ As already noted under the discussion of goats (4.19), sheep are frequently less prized than goats, and therefore it may seem strange in biblical texts to find sheep being given a preferential rating. What may appear even more difficult to understand is the suggestion that sheep are led by a shepherd rather than being driven. This fact may require some type of marginal note to accompany the text if people are to understand the basis for a number of similes and metaphors of the Scriptures. Furthermore, if the experience which people have of sheep is only their knowledge about wild sheep, then obviously references to the helplessness of sheep will be either meaningless or even contradictory. Again, a marginal note is in order.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πρόβατον[a] ‘sheep,’ 4.22) a follower of Christ, with the implication of needing care and guidance
glosses: a person who is like a sheep
senses.comment: Compare 11.29 and 11.31.

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: to formulate a future course of action
to cause a manifest state or condition of someone or something
the process of burning
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in the use of terms for burning. For example, the burning of a substance for light, as in the case of a lamp or candle, may be indicated by a term quite different from an expression indicating the destruction or burning up of something. Similarly, the burning of wood for cooking may require still another term. The extent or size of the fire involved may also require some distinctions in terms for burning.|It is important to indicate that in the phrase ‘her burning’ she is the one who is burned. One may therefore render this part of Revelation 18:18 as ‘when they see the smoke of the fire that burns her up.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πύρωσις[a] ‘to burn,’ 14.63) the experience of painful suffering
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πύρωσις in 1 Peter 4:12, see 78.37.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πύρωσις[a] ‘burning,’ 14.63) an exceptionally intense degree of some experience, with the implication of suffering
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πύρωσις in 1 Peter 4:12, see 24.91.

senses.def: (derivative of a base meaning literally ‘to be strong,’ ‘to be well,’ but used in the NT only as a formula for the ending of letters) to be well and to fare well
senses.comment: The occurrence of ῥώννυμαι as an epistolary formula may be understood in two different senses: either as a sincere expression of the wish that the person involved may fare well or merely as a device to indicate that the letter is complete. This second sense of ῥώννυμαι is treated in 33.24.

senses.def: to end a letter by means of the expression ἔρρωσθε (ἐρρώσσω in some manuscripts), always having a favorable connotation
senses.comment: Since in Acts 15:29 ἔρρωσθε ends a letter, it may be necessary in some languages to employ a typical letter-ending formula which will at the same time be favorable, for example, ‘with best wishes’ or ‘with sincere greetings.’ It would be quite wrong to use literally an expression such as ‘goodbye’ if this would be employed only or principally in direct address rather than at the end of a letter. For another interpretation of ἔρρωσθε in Acts 15:29, see 23.133.

senses.def: to suffer epileptic seizures (associated in ancient times with the supernatural power of the moon)

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a stubborn attitude with regard to any change in behavior
senses.comment: In a number of languages stubbornness may be described as ‘refusing to change’ or ‘refusing to think differently.’ In some instances stubbornness may be expressed idiomatically as ‘one’s heart only sees one thing’ or ‘one’s heart is blind’ or ‘one who always says No.’

senses.def: an open, oval area (frequently including a racetrack) around which was built an enclosed series of tiers of seats for those who came to watch the spectacles
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 9:24 the important feature is not the stadium as a construction, but as a place where races were conducted. Accordingly, ‘all the runners in the stadium’ may very well be rendered as ‘all the runners who are racing.’ The focus here is upon the competition rather than upon the type of place in which the competition took place.

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: the group of persons who are members of an extended family
senses.comment: This clause in Luke 1:61 may also be translated in some languages as ‘but you do not have anyone in your clan who has that name’ or ‘no one in your family has ever had that name’ or ‘none of your ancestors has ever had that name.’

senses.def: pertaining to feeling sympathy for someone or something
to join one’s witness to that of others
disorderly mob revolt, with special implications of uproar and disturbance
senses.comment: In a number of languages the meaning of ‘riot’ may be best expressed as ‘people shouting strongly against’ or ‘people shouting and fighting against’ or ‘a mob shouting against the government.’

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: a plan devised by a number of persons who agree to act against someone or some institution
senses.comment: See συνωμοσία 30.73 and its footnote.

senses.def: pertaining to a low probability of occurrence
one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem
a small opening (used in the NT only with reference to the so-called ‘eye’ of a needle)
senses.comment: The hole in a needle is variously referred to in different languages, for example, ‘the nostril of the needle,’ ‘the ear of the needle,’ ‘the mouth of the needle,’ and even ‘the anus of the needle.’

senses.def: a degree which exceeds extraordinarily a point on an implied or overt scale of extent
senses.comment: There are obviously a number of problems involved in attempting to render an expression of extraordinary degree, but it is sometimes possible to express such a degree by building up a series of intensive markers. For example, in Ephesians 2:7 one might translate τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ as ‘his very, very great grace,’ and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 one might render ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ as ‘God has very, very great power.’ Such expressions, however, may not do full justice to the intensity of degree expressed in ὑπερβάλλω and ὑπερβολή, since in a number of languages the closest equivalent might be something involving figurative meanings. For example, τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ in Ephesians 2:7 might be rendered as ‘he is gracious beyond anything we can imagine,’ and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ may be rendered as ‘God has power beyond any words to describe.’

senses.def: to continue to bear up despite difficulty and suffering
pertaining to love or affection for fellow believers
senses.comment: See discussion at 25.34.

senses.def: the psychological faculty of thoughtful planning, often with the implication of being wise and provident
the ability to understand, as the result of insight and wisdom
to be overtaken by or to experience stormy weather
senses.comment: In some languages it may be appropriate to translate χειμάζομαι in an idiomatic form, for example, ‘the wind and rain caught us’ or ‘the storm trapped us.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: skin or surface of the human body
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction must be made between the skin of an animal and the skin of a human being. A further distinction is often made between skin as a part of a living animal or human and skin which has been removed from the body and presumably made into leather (see δέρμα, 6.184).

senses.def: pertaining to a benefit to be derived from some ob ject, event, or state
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘benefit’ or ‘beneficial’ is often ‘that which helps.’ Accordingly, in 1 Timothy 4:8 one may render ἡ γὰρ σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστὶν ὠφέλιμος as ‘physical exercise helps to a small extent’ or ‘if one exercises one’s body, that helps a little.’
